extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy critics, and general readers interested in cultural criticism of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for how comedians and commentators should treat jokes about rape — when such material is harmful, how to respond, and what responsibilities influential comics carry. The piece argues for nuance, accountability, and consideration of targets and consequences rather than blanket censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the victim the target of the punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Think twice about who is the target of the punchline, and make sure it isn’t the victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that most commenters (especially feminists) are not asking to make rape off-limits but are asking that comics not direct jokes at victims. Example phrasing: “make sure it isn’t the victim.” Anti-pattern: punching down by targeting survivors or victims for laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer punching up (kick upward) rather than punching down
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift the target of transgressive humor upward toward those in power rather than toward vulnerable people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites calls to “kick upward” as the desired direction for comedy: be mindful of whether the joke attacks a powerless person or institution. Punching-up is presented as a qualitative standard for acceptable edginess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider victimization, trauma, and the consequences of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for victimization and the possible harm of trivializing trauma when making or defending jokes about rape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece lists concerns such as “victimization, consideration of words and their consequences, the general sexualizing of American culture” as central to the debate. This is a substantive criterion: weigh the real-world effects of language on survivors and cultural attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and nuance matter — avoid blanket bans or absolutist claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that critics are not calling for censorship in all circumstances; jokes about rape may be acceptable in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses it hasn’t found anyone arguing rape should never be joked about “under any circumstance.” The correct approach is nuanced assessment of context, target, and intent rather than categorical prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish criticism/accountability from censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing or advocating public critique of a comic’s material is not the same as seeking censorship; calling out is a legitimate social response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly rejects the straw-man that opponents want censorship. Instead, they frame responses (blogs, writing, public calling-out) as part of ongoing discourse and accountability, not suppression of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to answer to criticism and accept consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians should be ready to respond when people call them out for harmful jokes and, if warranted, change behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice: “whatever you’re gonna say, you’re gonna have to figure out a way to answer to it if you get called out.” Examples include public apologies (Dan Harmon) and revised practice (Oswalt, Louis C.K.). The expectation is responsiveness, not immunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination and willingness to change are virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians should examine their own biases and be willing to acknowledge when they were wrong and alter their approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt’s reversal is praised: he “examines his own biases and notions, and decides he’s been in error.” This criterion endorses reflective practice and public humility rather than defensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calling out a comedian who targets victims is an appropriate social response
rubrics_metrics.description: If someone makes a joke at the expense of a victim, it is legitimate to call them out and criticize them publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jim Norton conceded “someone who makes a joke at the expense of a victim to be called out as a dick.” The piece frames blogging, writing, and public critique as reasonable mechanisms to hold comics accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid straw-manning the debate (don’t misrepresent opponents as seeking censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce the argument to a false binary of free expression vs. censorship; engage with the substantive concerns being raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly praises destroying the dominant straw man: ‘No one is trying to make rape, as a subject, off-limits. No one is talking about censorship.’ Productive debate requires addressing victim-centered concerns instead of attacking critics as censorious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the cultural influence and responsibility of prominent comedians
rubrics_metrics.description: Influential comics’ choices about what to joke about shape broader cultural norms; they therefore carry responsibility for their material’s social impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that comedians like Oswalt, Maron, Louis C.K., and others are ‘influencers’ whose decisions ‘have an impact’ and ‘mold’ future comedy. This is a criterion to factor influence and ripple effects into decisions about material.
